concepts.title: The Parts of Our Body
concepts.explanation:
The best place to start learning about the body is your own body. It is right here with you.

Stand up. Touch the top of your head and say the word: head. Now move down, one part at a time. Touch your arms. Touch your hands. Touch your legs. Touch your feet. Say each name out loud as you touch it.

Now your face. Point to your eyes. Point to your ears. Point to your nose. Point to your mouth.

Now count. You have two eyes. Two ears. Two hands. Ten fingers. Ten toes. Count them slowly and see if you get the same number every time.

Each part of your body has a job to do. Your eyes see. Your ears hear. Your legs carry you. Your hands hold and carry things. All these parts work together, all day long, without you even asking them to.
concepts.example: Touch and name five parts of your body out loud: head, arms, hands, legs, feet. Then count your fingers and your toes.

concepts.title: Same and Different
concepts.explanation:
Here is a big and kind idea: all people have the same body parts, and yet every person looks a little different. Both things are true at the same time, and both are wonderful.

Look at the people in your home. What is the same? Everyone has a head. Everyone has two eyes, a nose, two hands and two feet. That is the same for every person in the whole world.

Now look again. What is different? Some hair is curly and some is straight. Some eyes are dark brown and some are lighter. Some people are tall and some are small. Some hands are big and some are little.

You and a grown-up both have two hands — that is the same. But your hands are small and their hands are big — that is different.

Being different is good. Every person is special. Nobody in the whole world is exactly like you. What a gift that is.
concepts.example: Look at two people in your home. Say one thing that is the same about them, and one thing that is different.

concepts.title: Our Five Senses
concepts.explanation:
Your body has special helpers called senses. They tell your brain about the world around you. You have five of them.

Sight comes from your eyes. Your eyes let you see colours, shapes, people and the bright sun. Look around and name what you can see — a cup, the door, a green plant. Now gently close your eyes and try to point at the door. It is much harder! Eyes help you a great deal.

Hearing comes from your ears. Tap a spoon on a cup, or clap your hands. Some sounds are happy, like a bird singing or your mother's voice. Some sounds warn us and keep us safe, like a loud beep.

Smell comes from your nose. Smell a piece of mango, a date, or some bread. Smell helps you enjoy good food, and it warns you too — if food smells bad, we do not eat it.

Taste comes from your tongue. A date tastes sweet.

Touch comes from your skin, especially your hands. Touch tells you if something is hot or cold, rough or smooth, hard or soft.

Sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch — five senses, working for you all day.
concepts.example: Close your eyes and ask someone to make a soft sound. Which sense did you use to find it? Now name all five senses and the body part each one uses.

concepts.title: Staying Healthy and Clean
concepts.explanation:
Your body is wonderful, and it is your job to take care of it.

Keeping clean is healthy, and it feels good too.

Washing your hands is the best place to start. Wet your hands. Rub in the soap. Make bubbles between your fingers. Scrub while you count slowly, so your hands get really clean. Then rinse the soap away.

When should you wash? Before you eat. After you use the toilet. And whenever your hands are dirty from playing.

Why does it matter? Because there are germs — tiny living things far too small for your eyes to see. If germs get onto your food and into your body, they can make you unwell. Soap and water wash them away.

Your body also needs good food, clean water, plenty of sleep and lots of moving and playing to stay strong.
concepts.example: Wash your hands with soap and count slowly to twenty while you scrub. Then say two times of day when washing hands is most important.

terms: Head
The top part of your body, above your neck.
Arms
The two long parts joined to your shoulders.
Legs
The two long parts you stand and walk on.
Hands
The parts at the end of your arms, used to hold things.
Feet
The parts at the end of your legs that you stand on.
Eyes
The body part we use to see.
Ears
The body part we use to hear.
Nose
The body part we use to smell.
Mouth
The body part we use to taste and to speak.
Senses
The five ways we learn about the world: see, hear, smell, taste and touch.

selfAssessment: I can point to and name parts of the body: head, arms, legs, hands and feet.
I can point to and name parts of the face: eyes, ears, nose and mouth.
I can name the five senses and the body part used for each.
I can say one way a sense helps to keep us safe.
I can sort objects using touch, such as soft and hard or rough and smooth.
I can say ways to keep our bodies clean and healthy.
